L24: ## In this article
L25: 
L37: ## cite3†About authentication L38: 
L39: Many REST API endpoints require authentication or return additional information if you are authenticated. Additionally, you can make more requests per hour when you are authenticated.
L40: To authenticate your request, you will need to provide an authentication token with the required scopes or permissions. There a few different ways to get a token: You can create a personal access token, generate a token with a GitHub App, or use the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` in a GitHub Actions workflow.
L41: After creating a token, you can authenticate your request by sending the token in the `Authorization` header of your request. For example, in the following request, replace `YOUR-TOKEN` with a reference to your token:
L42: 
L43:     `curl --request GET \
L44:     --url "https://api.github.com/octocat" \
L45:     --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR-TOKEN" \
L46:     --header "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10"
L47:     `
L48: 
L49: Note
L50: In most cases, you can use `Authorization: Bearer` or `Authorization: token` to pass a token. However, if you are passing a JSON web token (JWT), you must use `Authorization: Bearer`.
L51: ### cite9†Failed login limit L52: 
L53: If you try to use a REST API endpoint without a token or with a token that has insufficient permissions, you will receive a `404 Not Found` or `403 Forbidden` response. Authenticating with invalid credentials will initially return a `401 Unauthorized` response.
L54: After detecting several requests with invalid credentials within a short period, the API will temporarily reject all authentication attempts for that user (including ones with valid credentials) with a `403 Forbidden` response. For more information, see cite10†Rate limits for the REST API .
L55: ## cite4†Authenticating with a personal access token L56: 
L57: If you want to use the GitHub REST API for personal use, you can create a personal access token. If possible, GitHub recommends that you use a fine-grained personal access token instead of a personal access token (classic). For more information about creating a personal access token, see cite11†Managing your personal access tokens .
L58: If you are using a fine-grained personal access token, your fine-grained personal access token requires specific permissions in order to access each REST API endpoint. The REST API reference document for each endpoint states whether the endpoint works with fine-grained personal access tokens and states what permissions are required in order for the token to use the endpoint. Some endpoints may require multiple permissions, and some endpoints may require one of multiple permissions.
L59: For an overview of which REST API endpoints a fine-grained personal access token can access with each permission, see cite12†Permissions required for fine-grained personal access tokens .
L60: If you are using a personal access token (classic), it requires specific scopes in order to access each REST API endpoint. For general guidance about what scopes to choose, see cite13†Scopes for OAuth apps .
L61: Personal access tokens act as your identity (limited by the scopes or permissions you selected) when you make requests to the REST API. As such, it is important to keep your personal access tokens secure. For more information about keeping your personal access tokens secure, see cite14†Keeping your API credentials secure .
L62: ### cite15†Personal access tokens and SAML SSO L63: 
L64: If you use a personal access token (classic) to access an organization that enforces SAML single sign-on (SSO) for authentication, you will need to authorize your token after creation. Fine-grained personal access tokens are authorized during token creation, before access to the organization is granted. For more information, see cite16†Authorizing a personal access token for use with single sign-on .
L65: If you do not authorize your personal access token (classic) for SAML SSO before you try to use it to access a single organization that enforces SAML SSO, you may receive a `404 Not Found` or a `403 Forbidden` error. If you receive a `403 Forbidden` error, the `X-GitHub-SSO` header will include a URL that you can follow to authorize your token. The URL expires after one hour.
L66: If you do not authorize your personal access token (classic) for SAML SSO before you try to use it to access multiple organizations, the API will not return results from the organizations that require SAML SSO and the `X-GitHub-SSO` header will indicate the ID of the organizations that require SAML SSO authorization of your personal access token (classic). For example: `X-GitHub-SSO: partial-results; organizations=21955855,20582480`.
L67: ## cite5†Authenticating with a token generated by an app L68: 
L69: If you want to use the API for an organization or on behalf of another user, GitHub recommends that you use a GitHub App. For more information, see cite17†About authentication with a GitHub App .
L70: The REST API reference documentation for each endpoint states whether the endpoint works with GitHub Apps and states what permissions are required in order for the app to use the endpoint. Some endpoints may require multiple permissions, and some endpoints may require one of multiple permissions. For an overview of which REST API endpoints a GitHub App can access with each permission, see cite18†Permissions required for GitHub Apps .
L71: You can also create an OAuth token with an OAuth app to access the REST API. However, GitHub recommends that you use a GitHub App instead. GitHub Apps allow more control over the access and permission that the app has.
L72: 
L73: Access tokens created by apps are automatically authorized for SAML SSO.
L74: ### cite19†Using basic authentication L75: 
L76: Some REST API endpoints for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps require you to use basic authentication to access the endpoint. You will use the app's client ID as the username and the app's client secret as the password.
L77: For example:
L78: 
L79:     `curl --request POST \
L80:     --url "https://api.github.com/applications/YOUR_CLIENT_ID/token" \
L81:     --user "YOUR_CLIENT_ID:YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET" \
L82:     --header "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
L83:     --header "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10" \
L84:     --data '{
L85:       "access_token": "ACCESS_TOKEN_TO_CHECK"
L86:     }'
L87:     `
L88: The client ID and client secret are associated with the app, not with the owner of the app or a user who authorized the app. They are used to perform operations on behalf of the app, such as creating access tokens.
L89: 
L90: If you are the owner of a GitHub App or OAuth app, or if you are an app manager for a GitHub App, you can find the client ID and generate a client secret on the settings page for your app. To navigate to your app's settings page:
L91:   1. In the upper-right corner of any page on GitHub, click your profile picture.
L92:   2. Navigate to your account settings.
L93:      * For an app owned by a personal account, click Settings.
L94:      * For an app owned by an organization:
L95:        1. Click Your organizations.
L96:        2. To the right of the organization, click Settings.
L97:   3. In the left sidebar, click Developer settings.
L98:   4. In the left sidebar, click GitHub Apps or OAuth apps.
L99:   5. For GitHub Apps, to the right of the GitHub App you want to access, click Edit. For OAuth apps, click the app that you want to access.
L100:   6. Next to Client ID, you will see the client ID for your app.
L101:   7. Next to Client secrets, click Generate a new client secret to generate a client secret for your app.
L102: ## cite6†Authenticating in a GitHub Actions workflow L103: 
L104: If you want to use the API in a GitHub Actions workflow, GitHub recommends that you authenticate with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` instead of creating a token. You can grant permissions to the `GITHUB_TOKEN` with the `permissions` key. For more information, see cite20†Use GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication in workflows .
L105: If this is not possible, you can store your token as a secret and use the name of your secret in your GitHub Actions workflow. For more information about secrets, see cite21†Using secrets in GitHub Actions .
L106: ### cite22†Authenticating in a GitHub Actions workflow using GitHub CLI L107: 
L108: To make an authenticated request to the API in a GitHub Actions workflow using GitHub CLI, you can store the value of `GITHUB_TOKEN` as an environment variable, and use the `run` keyword to execute the GitHub CLI `api` subcommand. For more information about the `run` keyword, see cite23†Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions .
L109: In the following example workflow, replace `PATH` with the path of the endpoint. For more information about the path, see cite24†Getting started with the REST API .
L110: 
L111:     `jobs:
L112:       use_api:
L113:         runs-on: ubuntu-latest
L114:         permissions: {}
L115:         steps:
L116:           - env:
L117:               GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
L118:             run: |
L119:               gh api /PATH
L120:     `
L121: ### cite25†Authenticating in a GitHub Actions workflow using `curl` L122: 
L123: To make an authenticated request to the API in a GitHub Actions workflow using `curl`, you can store the value of `GITHUB_TOKEN` as an environment variable, and use the `run` keyword to execute a `curl` request to the API. For more information about the `run` keyword, see cite23†Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions .
L124: In the following example workflow, replace `PATH` with the path of the endpoint. For more information about the path, see cite24†Getting started with the REST API .
L125: YAML
L126: 
L127:     jobs:
L128:       use_api:
L129:         runs-on: ubuntu-latest
L130:         permissions: {}
L131:         steps:
L132:           - env:
L133:               GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
L134:             run: |
L135:               curl --request GET \
L136:               --url "https://api.github.com/PATH" \
L137:               --header "Authorization: Bearer $GH_TOKEN"
L138: 
L139: 
L140:     `jobs:
L141:       use_api:
L142:         runs-on: ubuntu-latest
L143:         permissions: {}
L144:         steps:
L145:           - env:
L146:               GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
L147:             run: |
L148:               curl --request GET \
L149:               --url "https://api.github.com/PATH" \
L150:               --header "Authorization: Bearer $GH_TOKEN"
L151:     `
L152: ### cite26†Authenticating in a GitHub Actions workflow using JavaScript L153: 
L154: For an example of how to authenticate in a GitHub Actions workflow using JavaScript, see cite27†Scripting with the REST API and JavaScript .
L155: 
L156: ## cite7†Authenticating with username and password L157: 
L158: Authentication with username and password is not supported. If you try to authenticate with user name and password, you will receive a 4xx error.

L116: # OAuth 2.0
L117: 
L118: OAuth 2.0 is a standard protocol that authorizes a client application (like a third-party app) to access specific resources on behalf of a user, without sharing the user’s password. It’s widely used for APIs that need secure, delegated access.
L119: 
L120: HighLevel supports the Authorization Code Grant flow with v2 APIs. Below is the step-by-step procedure to understand and use the OAuth 2.0 flow.
L121: 
L122: * * *
L123: ## 1. Register an OAuth Appcite62†​ L124:   1. Go to the cite63†Marketplace and sign up for a developer account.
L125:   2. Go to My Apps, click Create App.
L126:   3. Fill in the following details:
L127:      * APP Name: Suitable name for the app.
L128:      * APP Type: Private or Public.
L129:        * Private Apps: For personal/internal use, not listed in the Marketplace.
L130:        * Public Apps: Visible and installable by all users once approved.
L131: Note: We recommend starting with your app set to Private. This allows you to develop and thoroughly test its functionality in a controlled environment. Once you're confident the app is stable and complete, you can switch it to Public for broader installation and use by other accounts.
L132:      * Target User: This allows you to define who your app is intended for — in other words, who will actually be using it. For the vast majority of apps (approximately 95%), the ideal choice is `"Sub-account"` (recommended).
L133:      * Who can install: Who should be able to view and install the app from the Marketplace UI? The recommended setting is `“Both Agency & Sub-account”` to ensure maximum visibility and adoption of your app. However, if you’re building a fully white-labeled SaaS feature intended to be exclusively discovered and installed by agencies for use within their sub-accounts, you may choose to limit visibility to Agencies only.
L134:      * Listing Type: White-label recommended for marketing agencies.
L135: cite64†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L136:   4. After creating the APP you will be taken to the Profile section where you will need to add the details related to your APP. For eg; APP Logo, category, Company Name, APP Description, preview images etc.
L137:   5. After completing the profile details, please click on the Advanced Settings drop down available in the left pane and go to the auth section.
L138:   6. The Auth page will appear as shown in the screenshot below. This is where you’ll configure essential settings for your app’s OAuth integration, including scopes, redirect URLs, and client credentials.
L139: cite65†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L140: 
L141:   * Scopes: Scopes define the level of access your app will have — what data it can read or what actions it can perform on behalf of the user. cite6†Click Here to find all the available Scopes.
L142:     * It’s best practice to request the minimum number of scopes necessary for your app to function.
L143:     * Click on the "Select Scope" dropdown and choose the relevant scopes based on your app’s functionality.
L144:   * Redirect URL: A Redirect URL (also known as a Callback URL) is the destination where the authorization server will send the authorization code after the user installs the app.
L145:     * Enter your redirect URL in the Redirect URL field.
L146:     * Click the "Add" button to save it.
L147:   * Client Keys (ID & Secret): In the Client Keys section:
L148: 
L149:     * Click the "Add" button.
L150:     * Provide a name for your client key pair.
L151:     * Upon saving, your Client ID and Client Secret will be generated.
L152: 
L153: These credentials are used to identify and authenticate your application with the OAuth server during token exchange.
L154: Important: Be sure to copy and securely store your Client Secret immediately. After clicking "OK", you will not be able to view or copy the secret again from the UI.
L155: 
L156: * * *
L157: ## 2. Add the App to Your Desired Locationcite66†​ L158: 
L159:   * Have the location/agency admin visit your Installation URL.
L160:   * Select the location to connect.
L161:   * Redirected to your Redirect URL with an Authorization Code.
L162:   * Exchange the code for an Access Token via the OAuth 2.0 cite67†Get Access Token API.
L163:   * Use the Access Token to call APIs.
L164: 
L165: * * *
L166: ## 3. Get the Installation URLcite68†​ L167: 
L168: Inside your APP Auth Pane available inside the Advanced Settings Section you will be able to see the Install Link at the top of the Page.
L169: 
L170: cite69†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L171: 
L172: Click on the Show button and you will be able to see the Installation URLs which you will be using to install the APP.
L173: 
L174: cite70†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L175: Depending on your usecase and account setup you can either use the standard or the whitelabel version of the Installation URL.
L176: 
L177: Refer to the below steps to install the APP:
L178: 
L179:   1. Copy the Installation URL and open it in your browser.
L180:   2. In case you are not logged in to your GHL account it will ask you to login to your account.
L181: 
L182: cite71†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L183: 
L184:   * In case you are logged in it will show a page showcasing the accounts.
L185: 
L186: cite72†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L187:   3. Select the account you want to install the APP in.
L188:   4. When a user grants access, their browser is redirected to the specified redirect URI, and the Authorization Code is passed inside the code query parameter.
L189: 
L190:     `
L191: 
L192:     https://myapp.com/oauth/callback/highlevel?code=7676cjcbdc6t76cdcbkjcd09821jknnkj
L193: 
L194:     `
L195: This URL demonstrates a typical OAuth callback scenario for a HighLevel integration. The `code` parameter included in the query string is essential for completing the authorization flow.
L196: 
L197: * * *
L198: ## 4. Listening to Webhook Eventscite73†​ L199: 
L200: The HighLevel Marketplace App allows you to listen to various webhook events, enabling real-time updates and integrations based on user actions.
L201: 
L202: To set up webhook listeners:
L203:   1. Navigate to your app in the Marketplace dashboard.
L204:   2. Click on the "Advanced Settings" dropdown in the left-hand panel.
L205:   3. Go to the "Webhooks" section.
L206:   4. In the input box at the top, enter your webhook URL.
L207:   5. Use the toggle switches next to each event to subscribe to the events you wish to listen for.
L208: 
L209: For a full list of supported webhook events and example payloads, please refer to the documentation: cite61†Webhook Events & Payloads L210: ### Important: App Install Webhookcite74†​ L211: 
L212: One of the most critical webhook events is the App Install event. This event provides essential details whenever your app is installed by a user. If a webhook URL is configured for your app, this event is subscribed to by default.
L213: Here’s a sample payload for the App Install event:
L214: 
L215:     `
L216: 
L217:     {
L218: 
L219:       "type": "INSTALL",
L220: 
L221:       "appId": "665c6bb13d4e5364bdec0e2f",
L222: 
L223:       "versionId": "665c6bb13d4e5364bdec0e2f",
L224: 
L225:       "installType": "Location",
L226: 
L227:       "locationId": "HjiMUOsCCHCjtxzEf8PR",
L228: 
L229:       "companyId": "GNb7aIv4rQFVb9iwNl5K",
L230: 
L231:       "userId": "Rg6BRRiHh7dS9gJy3W8a",
L232: 
L233:       "companyName": "Marketplace and Integrations Prod Agency",
L234: 
L235:       "isWhitelabelCompany": true,
L236:       "whitelabelDetails": {
L237: 
L238:         "logoUrl": "https://...gif",
L239: 
L240:         "domain": "rajender.dentistsnear.me"
L241: 
L242:       },
L243: 
L244:       "timestamp": "2025-06-25T06:57:06.225Z",
L245: 
L246:       "webhookId": "1a533f85-1f1e-4886-891e-ee0cf4666e90"
L247: 
L248:     }
L249: 
L250:     `
L251: * * *
L252: ## 5. Exchange Authorization Code for Access Tokencite75†​ L253: 
L254: Once you have received the Authorization code on your redirect URl you are expected to use cite67†Get Access Token API endpoint to generate the Acces Token which you can then use to run the API endpoints.
L255: Sample Payload:
L256: 
L257:     `
L258: 
L259:     curl -X POST "https://services.leadconnectorhq.com/oauth/token" \
L260: 
L261:       -H "Accept: application/json" \
L262: 
L263:       -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
L264:

L310: ## 6. Refresh Token Usagecite76†​ L311: 
L312: As shown in the previous response, the Access Token expires after 86,399 seconds, which is approximately 24 hours. This means you'll need to regenerate a new Access Token once it expires to continue making API requests.
L313: 
L314: However, regenerating an Access Token using the authorization code requires repeating the entire installation process, which can be time-consuming. To simplify this, we also provide a Refresh Token along with the Access Token.
L315: The Refresh Token is valid for up to one year, or until it is used. Once you use a Refresh Token to obtain a new Access Token, the original Refresh Token becomes invalid, and the response will include a new Refresh Token along with the new Access Token. If left unused, the Refresh Token will remain valid for one year.
L316: 
L317: To generate a new Access Token using your existing Refresh Token, use the following API endpoint: cite67†Get Access Token L318:   * Access Tokens expire after ~24 hours.
L319:   * Refresh Tokens are valid for 1 year or until used.
L320:   * Use Refresh Token to obtain a new Access Token without reinstallation.
